findings.title: NewResourceServer now blocks synchronously on full index build during startup
findings.body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) directly in the constructor, which in turn calls searchSupport.init(), which builds the search index for every namespace returned by GetResourceStats before returning. Previously this cost was paid lazily inside the first gRPC call (with its own deadline); now it is paid unconditionally at construction time with no timeout. If NewResourceServer is invoked anywhere besides the dedicated storage-server module (e.g. during normal Grafana app-server bootstrap for unified storage), overall process startup can block for an arbitrarily long time while every namespace's index is built, and any failure during that build (e.g. a transient DB error) now causes server construction itself to fail outright rather than only a particular RPC. The PR description explicitly raises this as an open question ('What could this break?') but does not resolve it — there is no bound on index-build time nor any fallback/async option.

findings.title: Stop() no longer gates any RPC after shutdown
findings.body: Previously every RPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) called s.Init(ctx) first; since Init used sync.Once, after Stop() set s.initErr to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", those calls to Init(ctx) would surface that error to callers. This PR removes the s.Init(ctx) calls from all RPC handlers, so the initErr set in Stop() is now write-only dead state — no code path reads it anymore. As a result, after Stop() is called, in-flight or new RPCs will no longer get a clean 'service is stopping/stopped' error; they will instead proceed against a server whose background context (s.ctx) has already been cancelled (e.g. broadcaster/watch loops torn down), leading to inconsistent or silent failures instead of a clear error to the caller.

findings.title: Removing the full-function lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key
findings.body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu.Lock() for its entire duration, which incidentally serialized all builds, including two concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource key. The new code only takes cacheMu when writing the final result into b.cache (near the end of the function), so two goroutines can now run BuildIndex concurrently for the same key (this is a real possibility because searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex in search.go checks GetIndex and calls build() without any per-key lock, a gap already flagged by a TODO comment in that file). Concurrent builds for the same key can both call bleve.New()/bleve.NewMemOnly() and write documents independently, then race to overwrite b.cache[key], silently discarding one index's work or, for file-backed indexes sharing the same directory, causing on-disk index corruption/contention.

findings.title: TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu
findings.body: TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache directly without acquiring cacheMu (not even RLock), while BuildIndex now performs genuinely concurrent writes to b.cache under its own lock (enabled by the finer-grained locking introduced in this PR, combined with the worker pool in searchSupport.init that builds multiple namespaces in parallel). Because real concurrent map writes now happen during startup/runtime, a concurrent call to TotalDocs() (e.g. from a metrics scrape or another caller) racing with a BuildIndex write to the same map can trigger Go's 'concurrent map read and map write' fatal error, crashing the process. This hazard existed before but is made materially worse by the increased real concurrency this PR introduces for cache writes.

findings.title: Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed, losing coverage for the exact startup-init change
findings.body: This PR adds a skip for dbType == "postgres" in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer with only the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' No root cause or follow-up ticket is referenced. Since this PR's core change is moving unified-storage initialization into server startup (which can now block or fail at NewResourceServer time), disabling exactly the integration test that exercises a real storage-server startup against postgres removes the only regression coverage for that scenario, rather than investigating why it fails under the new init-at-startup behavior.
